components.text: Whether missing early witnesses leave changes introduced before surviving comparisons unknowable.
The decisive demand is whether absent early copies make the authors' wording inaccessible rather than merely less directly evidenced.
Whether numerous manuscripts fail to provide comparative control because the earliest ancestry is lost.
Whether versions and patristic quotations mitigate the evidentiary gap in early transmission.
The decisive demand is whether surviving witnesses provide sufficiently broad comparative evidence despite the lateness of most manuscripts.
A further demand concerns whether nonmanuscript witnesses materially constrain otherwise undocumented early transmission.
Whether textual variation generally obstructs substantial recovery rather than containing mostly trivial differences.
Whether the consequential minority includes prominent and interpretation-affecting passages.
The decisive demand is to characterize the significance of variation without allowing a small consequential class to be obscured by raw totals.
Whether the meaningful and viable subset is limited enough to permit substantial reconstruction.
Whether hundreds of disputed passages can affect interpretation to some degree.
The decisive demand is to acknowledge and delimit variants that are both viable and capable of affecting interpretation.
Whether consequential textual variants undermine essential Christian beliefs and practical textual trust.
Whether variants remain historically or interpretively significant apart from doctrinal effects.
The contacted component is whether disputed variants overturn essential Christian beliefs rather than whether they matter in every historical respect.
Whether alterations before the ancestry represented by surviving witnesses could leave no extant trace.
Whether the surviving alternatives ordinarily include the autographic reading.
The decisive demand is whether lost early transmission plausibly removed the authors' wording from all surviving alternatives.
A related demand is whether the surviving tradition retains original readings despite the lateness of most witnesses.
Whether missing early witnesses prevent warranted identification of the autographic wording.
Whether ordinary scholarship practically depends on sufficiently stable wording in most passages.
The contacted demand is whether sweeping textual unknowability coheres with detailed scholarship that relies on stable wording.
Whether percentages calculated from extant variants measure alterations introduced before the surviving manuscript tradition.
Whether the asserted ninety-nine-percent triviality addresses significant variants created before surviving witnesses.
The decisive demand is whether percentages calculated from extant variants can measure alterations predating the surviving manuscript ancestry.
The raw insignificance percentage also depends on the extant observed variant set.
Whether absence of effects on essential beliefs is sufficient to establish textual insignificance or trust.
The decisive demand is whether preservation of essential doctrines is the proper criterion for assessing textual and historical significance.
Whether extensive surviving evidence establishes that the earliest extant copies descend from accurate predecessors.
Whether extant triviality rates warrant claims about significant variants before surviving manuscripts.
The decisive demand is whether claims of ordinary extance establish that surviving readings descend through sufficiently accurate predecessors.
A further demand is whether observed insignificant variants constrain significant changes before extant witnesses.
The abundance claim must connect surviving witnesses to accurate early ancestry.
Whether the lost early copying period was wholly sparse and uncontrolled despite indirect evidence of circulation and copying.
Whether early use, multiple copying, versions, and patristic evidence make accurate ancestry probable.
Whether diverse nonmanuscript witnesses materially supplement the surviving manuscript base.
The decisive demand is whether any indirect evidence connects surviving witnesses to repeated and distributed early copying.
The missing direct copies leave a demand for evidence that the early period was not wholly sparse or linear.
The reply invokes early copying and multiple witness forms rather than relying only on medieval numerical abundance.
Whether the absence of hard evidence prevents any warranted probability of accurate early textual ancestry.
Whether indirect evidence can support essential recovery despite the acknowledged early evidentiary gap.
Whether evidence outside extant variant percentages can support the recovery conclusion.
The decisive demand is whether the absence of hard early controls precludes a probabilistic warrant based on cumulative indirect evidence.
The reply must acknowledge the direct evidentiary gap while explaining why it is not dispositive.
A related demand is whether evidence beyond observed extant percentages supports the conclusion.
Whether reconstructing the ancestor of surviving witnesses establishes identity with the author’s original wording.
Whether identifying tampering within surviving comparisons establishes access to the autograph itself.
Whether the recovered initial text and the autographic text can be treated as equivalent without an added warrant.
The decisive demand is whether reconstructing the ancestor of surviving witnesses establishes identity with the author's original wording.
Detecting alteration relative to an earlier reading does not by itself identify that reading as autographic.
Essential recovery still requires a bridge from reconstructed initial text to authorial wording.
Whether unspecified indirect evidence satisfies the affirmative burden to warrant textual trust.
Whether the cited circulation evidence establishes competent early copyists and high-quality exemplars.
Whether present textual recoverability establishes the quality of lost ancestral exemplars.
The decisive demand is whether unspecified indirect evidence satisfies the advocate's burden to warrant textual trust.
The competence of early copyists and quality of exemplars remain necessary considerations in evaluating the cumulative case.
Ordinary extance claims must rest on a warranted connection to reliable early ancestry.
What evidentiary standard the affirmative must satisfy before historical textual trust is warranted.
Whether responsible confidence requires hard proof of accurate copying at every lost stage.
Whether probabilistic identity can be warranted despite the conceptual initial-original distinction.
The decisive demand is what evidentiary standard the advocate must satisfy before historical textual trust is warranted.
The ancestry warrant should be probabilistic rather than a demand for absolute historical certainty.
The initial-original distinction remains relevant but need not impose certainty as the threshold for responsible trust.
